paragraphs.heading: A straight-line graph
paragraphs.text: In calculus, a linear function is one whose graph is a straight line. In terms of polynomials, it has degree one or less, which takes in constant polynomials and also the zero polynomial. It is written using two constants, a and b, which are often real numbers. With one variable, its graph is a line that is never vertical. The constant a is usually called the slope of the line, and b is called the intercept.

paragraphs.heading: Which way it tilts
paragraphs.text: The sign of a tells you how the line leans. When a is greater than zero, the slope is positive and the graph rises; when a is less than zero, the slope is negative and the graph falls. A constant function counts as linear here too, because it is a polynomial of degree zero or the zero polynomial. With one variable, its graph is a flat, horizontal line.

paragraphs.heading: A second meaning
paragraphs.text: The same phrase means something else in linear algebra, mathematical analysis and functional analysis. There, it names a type of function from one vector space to another, and it preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication. To keep the two ideas apart, the calculus kind is often called an affine function instead. Seen from linear algebra, polynomial functions whose degree is 0 or 1 are exactly the scalar-valued affine maps. Some authors save the name linear function for linear maps whose values are scalars, though these are more often called linear forms.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of plus
paragraphs.text: In this setting, a stands for a constant taken from the field of scalars, such as the real numbers. The inputs x and y are elements of a vector space V, which might simply be the scalars themselves. One plus sign can hide two different operations. Adding x and y inside V need not be the same operation as adding f(x) and f(y) inside W, the space where the function's values live.

paragraphs.heading: Where the meanings meet
paragraphs.text: The two meanings overlap in one case. A calculus linear function is also a linear map exactly when its value at zero is zero, which is the same as saying the constant b equals zero. On a graph, that means the line has to pass through the origin. So a line with a nonzero intercept b is an affine function but not a linear map.
